speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Andre that Bill C-22, an Act to amend the Patent Act and to provide for certain matters in relation thereto, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee; and the amendment of Mrs. Killens (p. 1378).

Mr. Speaker, the Bill before us today, Bill C-22, a Bill that will amend the Patent Act, is an example of one of the more shoddy ways the Government has bowed down to pressure from American corporations by putting the interests of multinational corporations ahead of the interests of Canadians. This is occurring in an area which is extremely important. All people will need access to drugs at some time in their lives. Our population is aging and will require the increased use of drugs. Yet the Government is introducing and trying to push through legislation which will result in rather substantial increases in the cost of drugs.
Let us look at how we got ourselves into this situation. In recent years, Canadians have seen a diminution in the price of drugs as a result of very specific legislation. Canadians are very upset at the thought that those advantages will soon be lost if this legislation is passed.
In the bad old days when there was no competition from generic drugs, drug prices in Canada were enormously high. In the 1960s, the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission in 1963, the Hall Royal Commission on Health Services in 1964, and the Harley Special Committee of the House of Commons on Drug Costs and Prices in 1967 all investigated the pharmaceutical industry in Canada. These three major inquiries agreed that drug prices were too high and that government action was required to bring them down and to stimulate price competition.
The Hall Commission concluded that Canadian drug prices were among the highest in any industrialized nation in the world. All three inquiries felt that it was the foreign-based multinational drug companies that were dominating the Canadian drug industry and using their 17-year patent periods to set prices which were too high.
The Restrictive Trade Practices Commission recommended complete abolition of drug patents, a very strong remedy indeed. The Hall Commission and the Harley Committee recommended a compromise policy designed to stimulate price competition while maintaining the principle of patent protection but a reduced patent protection allowing companies that wished to import and sell generic equivalents of patented brand names to do so upon receipt of a compulsory licence and the payment of a royalty. This compromise was indeed
November 24, 1986

legislated in 1969 and became Section 41(4) of the Patent Act. This, of course, is the section that is at risk now.
Since that time, multinational corporations have attacked compulsory licensing and they have stepped up the attack in recent years. I recall being a part of the Canadian delegation to the United Nations a couple of years ago. While we were in New York, American multinational companies took the occasion to lobby Canadian legislators. I must say that I was ashamed by the behaviour of Conservative members of that delegation who simply listened respectfully to the multinationals and said: "Yes, sir, you are unhappy with what we are doing with pharmaceuticals, we will change it". This occurred very soon after the 1984 election, so Conservative members said to the multinationals: "Just give us a chance. It will not take us long to do what you want but we have only just come into office. We can assure you that you will get the kind of legislation that you want". Of course, what they were saying was that the interests of American multinationals would be put ahead of the interests of the Canadian people.
I am getting ahead of my chronology somewhat. In 1984, the federal Government appointed Professor Harry Eastman of the University of Toronto to head a commission of inquiry on the pharmaceutical industry. His report, which was released in May of 1985, recommended that we retain compulsory licensing. However, he proposed that patent holders be guaranteed four years of exclusivity and freedom from competition and that companies that actually do research in Canada be able to receive royalties higher than the current 4 per cent. Again, that was something of a compromise but one which did maintain the principle that compulsory licensing would be, if modified, nonetheless continued.
Since the introduction of compulsory licensing in 1969, drug companies have still, of course, enjoyed enormous growth and very adequate profits. The idea that this measure created a difficulty for them is not supported by any factual investigation. On that, the Eastman Report said:
An overall summary of the comparison of the growth and development of the pharmaceutical industry in Canada relative to that of the United States yields the straightforward conclusion that growth has been more buoyant in Canada than it has been in the United States since 1967.
If compulsory licensing had completely ruined the industry, this would not be the case. The idea that we should adopt the American model for growth is simply not borne out.
Again, the Eastman Report said:
Compulsory licensing has not had a discernible negative impact on the profitability and rate of growth of the pharmaceutical industry in Canada as a whole.
That is pretty clear as well.
We have seen pharmaceutical companies take legal action to try to get even higher profits by challenging the compulsory licensing provisions. A decision was made in November, 1985 involving a multinational drug company's challenge to this section of the Patent Act under the Charter of Rights. At that time, the Federal Court stated that there was no information to demonstrate that compulsory licensing was denying either
Patent Act
the multinational companies or their Canadian subsidiaries a reasonable return on their investments. So much for the contention that compulsory licensing has been harmful to the industry and the contention that there has been any unfairness.
On June 30, 1986, the former Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs released the Government's draft amendments to the Patent Act outlining the provisions we are studying today. These provisions were, of course, brought in under a great deal of pressure. I already noted the example of drug companies lobbying parliamentarians directly. Of course, we know that they have lobbied the American Government and have managed to get President Reagan to take up the issue, indeed at the highest level, with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) himself.
The issue was discussed at the 1985 and 1986 so-called Shamrock Summits. We know that the Prime Minister agreed to knuckle under to the American pressure at that time. The pressure continued as the Government did not respond fast enough. In early April, 1986, the United States Trade Representative, Clayton Yeutter, rapped Canada's knuckles for failing to honour the commitments made by the Government through the Prime Minister by saying that the drug issue "-should have been resolved a long time ago. We've been exercising uncommon patience. But even our patience ultimately begins to wear thin". That was pretty heavy-handed indeed, and I am sorry to see that anyone would respond to it.
In late April when President Reagan's plan for so-called fast-track free trade negotiations with Canada ran into trouble, the drug industry in the United States actively lobbied committee members to go along with the President and the Canadian Government. We have seen how the talks on free trade have been brought into play in this issue as well. On several occasions in 1986, the Government appeared to be on the brink of giving in to pressure but backed away. Ultimately, the Government did capitulate.
The Bill before us raises many questions. The commission of inquiry into the pharmaceutical industry found that profit levels of multinationals were higher than in most home countries including Switzerland, West Germany, the United Kingdom, France and Japan, all major producers in the industry. The one exception to that was the United States which has had among the highest drug prices in the world. Of course, Canada provides tax incentives to research which are among the most generous in the world.
The manner in which this legislation is supposed to operate assumes that decisions are made a certain way within the companies as to where they will do their research and where they will produce their product. Drug manufacturing breaks down into two phases. The first is the making of the active ingredients, the chemicals themselves. Then there is the preparation of the final formulation, including combining the active ingredients with various inactive ingredients: colourings,

November 24, 1986
Patent Act
flavourings, stabilizers, packaging, labelling, and those aspects of the final preparation of the drugs.
At the present time, almost no active ingredient manufacturing takes place in Canada. Both the patent holding and the generic companies import their active ingredients. Then they do some of their final stage manufacturing in Canada. That holds true for both the generics and the patent drugs. I think that we have to understand that.
A few small countries have developed active ingredient manufacturing industries to serve world markets for generic drugs. Generic companies in Canada have the right to apply for compulsory licences to manufacture the active ingredients. This right has existed since 1923. But they do not very often do so because the Canadian market is too small to make such an operation viable.
The failure of the 1923 policy to create drug price competition in 1969 led to the creation of compulsory licences to import because we did not have domestic production. We know that often a single factory in one particular country meets a company's world-wide markets. Usually these factories are located in the multinational's home country, or in some place like Ireland or Puerto Rico that offer particularly generous tax breaks, and sometimes tariff-free access to major markets. So there are these structural reasons in the industry itself.
While we cannot expect a big change as a result of the legislation that we have before us, these are conditions that we have known about for some time.
Despite all of this, the federal Government claims that the Bill before us will stimulate both generic and multinational firms to make the active ingredients in Canada. This claim rests on the provisions of the Bill that generic companies will still be able to acquire compulsory licences to manufacture generic active ingredients in Canada, although subject to qualification. Patent holding companies can avoid this type of generic competition if they notify the Commissioner of Patents that they intend to make the patented active ingredient in Canada completely or substantially to meet Canadian demand. If they do notify the Commissioner, they must begin manufacturing within two years, or risk losing their market exclusivity.
It is not at all clear to me why generic companies would manufacture more active ingredients in Canada under this Bill than they did between 1923, when they could have done so, and up until 1969, when the patent legislation was changed. Why are we bringing in a provision that has already been tried for more than 40 years, and it did not result in domestic manufacturing of the active ingredients? We can have no optimism that that will change now.
With regard to the final product manufacturing, there is every reason to expect that multinational companies will invest in plant expansions in Canada within the next few years, regardless of whether or not this Bill before us today is passed. These are the trends. There is an increase in the demand for drugs. There is a change in the demographics. There are more elderly people with health care concerns and people needing
drugs. We would otherwise have expected to see this type of expansion, with no thanks to this legislation whatsoever. Yet there is no confidence that the legislation will bring about the change in the manufacturing of the active ingredients themselves.
The Government has made many claims that this legislation will improve research and development in Canada. We must look at those claims. I am sure our Party would be very partial to legislation that would improve research and development in Canada. Unfortunately, when we examine more closely what the Bill says, this result will not happen either. Canada has very little basic research. This was true in the pharmaceutical industry in the period prior to 1969 as well as since. We have no reason to believe that the same pharmaceutical companies that were not doing research and development before 1969, when there was no generic drug legislation, would suddenly do it now.
In 1983, only about 15 per cent of research and development expenditures by pharmaceutical firms were for basic research. That is considerably less than 1 per cent of the value of those firms' sales in Canada. That is a pretty shameful record indeed. It is pretty typical of countries whose pharmaceutical industries are dominated by the subsidiaries of multinationals.
The levels of drug research and development in Canada are similar to those of some other small countries which do not have independent non-multinationals or their own pharmaceutical industries.
Most pharmaceutical research in Canada involves clinical testing of a drug's safety and effectiveness. That is simply to meet requirements of our own health and drug legislation. It is not basic research. It is simply to meet the requirements of the Food and Drugs Act.
Despite these well-known facts, the federal Government claims that its draft Bill contains "strong new incentives" for research. I would like to quote what the Government has stated:
Drugs invented and manufactured in Canada will receive full 17-year patent monopolies.
If the Government is not satisfied with the industry's research investments by 1990, it may remove some or all of the exclusivity granted under the Act.
The federal Government claims that the new policy will turn Canada into "a world-class centre for the research, development, and manufacture of pharmaceuticals".
Unfortunately, these very fine hopes entirely ignore the conclusions of the federal commission of inquiry that Canada is not well placed to become a major world centre for pharmaceutical research, or for the production of active chemical ingredients for the very reasons that I have just related. We have these multinational companies, and it is not their practice to do research and development, or indeed to manufacture the active ingredients in smaller countries. In the case of research and development, they do it in their home country. They do the manufacturing under very specific conditions.
November 24, 1986

The question of drug prices has been pretty hotly debated in the House over the last weeks. It is being considered very actively by the Canadian public. We have had extremely outlandish statements by the Government that this new legislation will not result in an increase in drug prices.
The generic competition stimulated by the 1969 amendment has saved Canadian consumers hundreds of millions of dollars. This has been calculated at $211 million for 1983 alone. Of course, when added up over the years, it is into the billions of dollars that Canadians have been spared by having generic drug competition.
We have a Minister who claims that the new policy will not cause drug prices to rise, indeed that the new policy will not cause an increase of even one cent in drug prices. On the other hand, when you get down to the fine print, the Government has to admit such things as, and I quote, that it "may, however, result in a delay of the price reductions associated with the introduction of new generic drugs".
This is a pretty roundabout way of admitting that when a new drug comes on to the market there is the four-year period of protection. After that the prices go down. So you must look at the costs at least over a 10-year period. If you look at a 10-year period, you will see that prices are indeed considerably lower under the condition of generic drug competition than with the monopoly situation that the Government wishes to reintroduce.
Canadian consumers can expect substantially higher drug costs during the 10-year delay in the introduction of new generic drugs. I note that the federal Government's published cost estimates for the new policy stop at 1990. This is a convenient place to stop, because the Government does not want to admit that the prices are then going to go up. Reductions that would otherwise have happened because of generic competition simply will not happen. That drug competition which the 1969 policy brought in will have ended.
Despite its claims about drug prices, the federal Government has nevertheless promised to pay the provincial Governments $100 million in transitional payments by 1991.1 think that this rather embarrassingly belies the argument that there will not be any increases. Why is the federal Government handing over $100 million if there will not be any increases? Any person with common sense will certainly be asking that.
It will be very scant consolation to Canadian taxpayers to know that they will be subsidized through federal taxes instead of provincial taxes. The money will go to provincial Governments so that they can pay the multinational corporations for these increased prices. The point is that increased prices will hurt. If it means that provincial Governments have to pay more for their particular medicare costs, then the federal Government will have to pay more. Even if it is not the individual consumer, we know that these costs have to be borne.
Patent Act
We expect the Government will then say that the cost of drugs has risen and that medicare is costing too much money. In that event, it will be required to cut back somewhere else in the medicare system. It will have to cut other services to make up for the increased costs of drugs.
Of course we do not want to see that happening. We do not want to see medicare hurt. We do not want to see other services being cut back as a result of increased prices in pharmaceutical products.
In winding up my remarks, let me point out that the proposal of the Government for a regulatory board to look at drug prices is not a satisfactory option. It is not clear how much authority the board will have. The Bill provides for provincial and federal health Ministers to intervene in hearings. However, there is no provision for consumers or other public interest groups. It is a very unsatisfactory business altogether. We will have another bureaucracy to carry out a policy which is not as good as the present one.
I urge Hon. Members to look at the past progress with generic drug competition and the enormous savings for Canadians as a result of the policy. I ask them to reject this extremely misguided approach which puts the welfare of American multinational pharmaceutical companies ahead of the needs of Canadians for decent drug prices and adequate competition in the pharmaceutical industry to ensure that prices remain at a reasonable level.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald). We heard the Minister say that he would bring information to us in committee but that he would not bring us specific documents relating to the costs or an analysis of the costs which will be faced by consumers. Would the Hon. Member speculate on why the Government does not want to release those documents?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) raises an extremely important question. She will know that her colleagues and members of my Party have raised with the Government in Question Period the need to have the documents tabled so that Canadians and consumer and advocacy groups can look at the cost estimates.
She will also know that the Government indicated that it would not cost a cent more but that it would not provide the information which gives specific estimates as to the costs in particular years. This must be a fraudulent claim, if the documentation is not to be put before Members of the House and the Canadian public.
A Government which really had hard information showing that prices would not rise would be delighted to document it and to hand over its study results. We have to be entirely suspicious of a Government which uses taxpayers' money to collect information and then denies Members of the House and the Canadian public access to the information on which they

November 24, 1986
Patent Act
can make their own reasoned assessments and reach their own conclusions.

Mr. Speaker, could the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood also elaborate on some of the reasons the Government would see fit in certain instances to inform some multinational drug companies of what was coming up in the way of legislation without letting Hon. Members of the House have that same information?

Mr. Speaker, indeed the Hon. Member for Hamilton East raises a touchy question. I hope the Government was extremely embarrassed to have this information come out. Multinational corporations were given information which Canadian parliamentarians were not given. This coincides with my own experience of seeing government Members lobbied by representatives of the same interest and seeing them completely willing to capitulate. They were willing to put second the interest of Canadians and to put first the pressure from American multinational corporations. It is shameful. The incident to which the Hon. Member referred is simply the last in a very shameful series of incidents of this nature.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a number of questions for the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald). She might answer any or all of them, if there is time.
Could she tell the House when the last drug was invented in Canada? I think she will find that it goes back a great many years, partly because the system as it is now provides no incentive whatsoever to discover drugs which perhaps her mother or my mother might need. We are trying to create an atmosphere in the Bill where the Japanese will not have a drug which we do not have in Canada.
Perhaps the Hon. Member does not understand that $600 million has been committed by the drug industry for research and development and product development in Canada because of the Bill. I do not know how many thousands of jobs it will mean in Toronto, but I am sure her city will receive a lot of them.
The main point of the Hon. Member's speech was that prices will rise under the Bill. It is very clear that the prices of existing drugs will not rise as a result of the Bill. What is happening is that they are speculating about drugs which may be on the market in 1995 or whenever. How can the Hon. Member feel that the Bill will make prices higher in 1995 than they would have been otherwise?
Also I wish the Hon. Member would say something about the recent Eastman Report which recommended balancing the interests of consumers like her mother and my mother with the interest in getting some new development of drugs in Canada. The Hon. Member might know that presently people are simply filling bags in Toronto, Montreal, Edmonton or wherever. No research is being done. Nothing is being developed. This is why the situation is intolerable.
Britain, Germany, Switzerland, and a great many other countries think that Canada has been acting in a highly irresponsible way for many years. It is time we grew up and did things in the same way as the rest of the industrialized world.

Mr. Speaker, in the very short time left to me, let me touch upon the questions raised by the Parliamentary Secretary. Turning to the question about higher drug prices, certainly Dr. Eastman said that the prices would be going up because there would not be reductions as would happen under generic drug competition. As soon as the generics come on to the market, there is competition and prices fall. This process will not happen in the future if the Bill is passed.
Let us turn to the question about the discovery of drugs. Of course it is a very important one. We would be very sympathetic to legislation if we thought it would result in increased research and development and the invention of new drugs in Canada. There is no reason to think that that will happen because there are structural reasons for how multinational corporations decide to do their research.
In the very long period of time between 1923 and 1969 very little research was done in Canada. The change in generics only came about in 1969. If the Hon. Member wants to make the point that there has not been enough drug discovery in Canada, then he must explain why it did not happen before 1969 when the same conditions held as the Government proposes for after 1986 or whenever the legislation is adopted.
The question of jobs is a very tricky one. Naturally we would like to see more jobs created in research and development and manufacturing. However, I note that there are no firm guarantees. An exchange of letters is no guarantee whatsoever. We have seen shameful examples in the past of corporations being given fantastic hand-outs, taking their profits and running. The problem is in the structure of multinational corporations. They do not have the incentive to do that work in Canada.
With increasing prices in drugs, money will go out of the economy. Money which goes in profits to multinational corporations will result in job loss. It is money which Canadian consumers, either directly or through their health plans, will be paying. It will go into increased profits outside Canada and to the headquarters of multinational corporations. That is money that might otherwise be staying in Canada and creating jobs here. We have to expect a net job loss as a result of the adoption of the legislation before us today.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I regret to inform the House that the period for questions and comments has now terminated. Debate. The Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins).
November 24, 1986

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in the debate on this very important Bill and to express my support for Bill C-22 which the Minister has brought forward and to disagree with the amendment under debate.
I found it interesting listening to the debate and to the questions that have been asked in the 14 to 15 hours of discussion in this House on this issue because so much of it is based on either false information or what appears to be a desire to either scare or misinform the public about the real intentions and impact of this legislation.
We know that this is not a new subject. The previous speaker spoke about the history and the development of patent protection. I would like to bring Members back to 1982. In June of that year there was a debate in this House on patent protection. The then Minister of State for Science and Technology, Mr. Roberts, said:
The Government is very concerned about the over-all low level of research and development in the private sector and is actively pursuing a number of measures to improve Canada's performance in this area. We recognize the importance which a strong patent system can play in encouraging industrial investment in R and D thus creating the appropriate climate for innovation.
On that same day the former Liberal Member for Scarborough East said:
With the return of Great Britain to patent protection, Canada remains the only developed country with this unique discouragement to product innovation and manufacturing in the pharmaceutical industry.
This is not a new debate, Mr. Speaker. When the roles were reversed, our colleagues across the floor in the Liberal Party were asking for this kind of patent protection. But it was not only the members of the Official Opposition. I recall that in November, 1982-Members may check back in the records of Hansard-our colleague in the New Democratic Party, the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), raised in the House the following concern:
The transfer will mean the lay-off of some 300 employees, many of them fulltime researchers at the lab.
Obviously he was referring to a situation in his own riding. He then questioned the Minister and said:
1 would like to know from the Minister what action the Government is going to take to make sure we can do this pharmaceutical research in our own country.
The then Minister for Economic Development, the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount, (Mr. Johnston), replied:
1 am hopeful, as are my colleagues, that in the very near future we will have something that will enable us to retain this very important expertise in the area of science and technology.
There was a recognition of the problem and we knew that the amendments put through in 1969 had had a detrimental impact on research and development in Canada. We know that these amendments were totally unfair and inconsistent with what was happening right around the world; we knew that changes needed to be made. There were committees and commissions meeting on the subject, but basically there was no action. People were concerned about the difficult and complex
Patent Act
issue, but it is no easy task to ensure that the public understands it, so no action was taken. We remained behind not only the rest of the western world but behind countries in Asia, in the Pacific Rim and even Taiwan which have patent protection. Nevertheless, we just toddled along in our way and nothing was done until our Government, after reviewing the situation, brought forward legislation to remedy it. It is important legislation which tries to be fair to all of the parties involved.
I share the conviction of the Hon. Minister that these amendments, to the compulsory licensing provision of the Patent Act will correct the disservice which arose out of the 1969 amendments which largely ignored the role of research and development in the pharmaceutical industry. These amendments will address the situation and, in time, Canada will become one of the world's leaders in research. Not only will Canada's status as a research oriented country be enhanced, allowing it to compete on a realistic basis in the future of research and development investments, but individual Canadians will benefit, as consumers of pharmaceutical products and as a result of increased employment generated by these amendments. That is something about which we have heard a great deal in the debate. It is not just wishful thinking. The Minister has produced.
Just recently in Vancouver, in my own home province, a biomedical research institution has announced that it will be investing $40 million in research through the University of British Columbia. This will create in itself 50 technical, professional jobs, and we all know the kinds of spin-offs that come with that kind of employment as well. A new centre for biomedical research in Vancouver will be created.
A recent announcement by the University of Alberta was for $100 million. There were other announcements in central Canada, Quebec and Ontario of projects that will be going ahead as a result of these proposed changes. These will create jobs and ensure that we are to fulfil the commitment and expectation the Minister has mentioned of research and development increasing by $1.4 billion. Three thousand jobs will be created as a result of the changes. That is a lot of jobs in your riding, Mr. Speaker, in my riding and right across the country, and it is in one of the areas in which we need to concentrate.
May I digress for a moment, Mr. Speaker. At the First Ministers' Conference in Vancouver which I had the opportunity to attend, the Premier of Ontario, Mr. Peterson, was talking about the high priority that must be placed on science and technology, that we had to make this the field on which to concentrate in the future. Our Government has shown we support that kind of a priority. We are undertaking the kind of legislative changes to encourage it. But all my colleagues across the way who are members of the same Party as Mr. Peterson can utter is doom and gloom. It is complete nonsense, Mr. Speaker.
Let me refer to The Globe and Mail. Many of us on this side of the House are not totally happy with some of the articles

November 24, 1986
Patent Act
and editorials in The Globe and Mail. In an editorial in the November 18, 1986, issue the writer understood what the Government was doing through this legislation and was certainly supportive. It talked about international concerns and reads:
If gentle, first-world Canada opts out of patent protection for certain products, what are the prospects for the rest of the world? The new round of talks at the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade has identified intellectual property rights as a priority for new agreements. Canada's isolationism on pharmaceuticals is a troubling aberration among industrial states committed to fair play in international trade.
That opinion, Mr. Speaker, is also supported by comments I received last week when I attended a meeting at the Pacific Economic Co-operation Conference held in Vancouver with representatives from all of the Asian countries. One of the major priorties in addition to agriculture in discussions in the new round of talks on tariffs and trade on which we have to cooperate with the Pacific Rim countries were issues related to intellectual property. But how can Canada play a meaningful role in these kinds of meetings on these kinds of issues if we ourselves have not taken the steps to bring Canada into line in providing protection for intellectual property, something which this Bill will do? I am pleased that not only in previous incarnations were my hon. friends on the other side of the House agreeing with the principle of what we are doing, but that our country's leading newspaper, The Globe and Mail, also agrees with what we are doing.
Since Canada does not provide the same protection for intellectual property in this field as do all other industrialized countries, research and development activity by the pharmaceutical industry has stagnated. In other countries full protection for intellectual properties has generated enormous investments. Canada has missed out on investments it might have shared in had we provided a better environment and system of incentives for investing in research.
I would like to turn to another aspect of this issue which has received a great deal of attention. We know that the 1969 compulsory licensing amendments did produce savings for Canadian consumers of pharmaceutical products. The changes the Government is introducing to compulsory licensing will continue to provide Canadians with price savings while generating significant employment in research, development and manufacturing. In fact, the amendment to create a Drug Prices Review Board will provide more complete price protection for Canadians than has been possible until now. The 1969 amendments relied soley on the introduction of generic drugs to provide price competition and to lower the price of these products. If no generic drugs existed, there was no means of price competition. In effect, this means that no price competition existed from anywhere from five years to 15 years. This was the time it took for a generic product to reach the market. In addition, there are certain types of medicines which are never copied and, hence, there is no price competition.
I recommend that my colleagues look at the amendments just introduced. They help ensure fairer drug prices by providing for price reviews even before the generic products become available. Perhaps that is a point which has been missed. I emphasize that with Bill C-22 there will be price reviews for all patented drugs, not only those that are copied. This is a significant step forward in providing protection for Canadian consumers.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I seek your guidance, but I just noted that it is past five o'clock. Normally we would be proceeding to Private Members' Hour at this time. I understand that we are not going to Private Members' Hour today because a member of the Conservative Party is off visiting in South Africa on a private trip.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The House was properly informed on Friday of what is happening here today. I do not think that was necessary. The Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins) has the floor on debate.

Mr. Speaker, I will continue because I think all Members of the House have a great deal of interest in this Bill. I am pleased that we have an additional hour in which to debate it.
In order to make Canadian intellectual property laws similar to those in other industrialized countries, patentees of pharmaceutical products will be provided with up to 10 years of market exclusivity. Furthermore, the commission of inquiry into the pharmaceutical industry reported that it has taken on average 11.5 years from the time the original drug is introduced on the market until the generic copy is sold. The proposed 10 years is, therefore, really not far out of line with the present situation.
Let me remind Hon. Members that generic firms will not have to wait for seven years to apply for a licence. They can apply for and receive a licence for a drug at any time. They will simply not be able to sell the drug in Canada for a specified period of time. The fact that they have the licence will help minimize any delays in getting a generic product to market once the appropriate period of protection has ended. Seven years after the drug is first introduced on the Canadian market the generic drug companies will be permitted to activate their licences to manufacture, and after 10 years they can import the drug without any restriction.
By making the period of protection shorter for manufacturing licences than for licences to import, the Government is maximizing the employment benefits for Canadians and maximizing the opportunities for the manufacture of fine chemicals industry in Canada. If these periods did not differ, there would be no incentive to actually manufacture the drug and/or its ingredients in Canada, and the benefit to Canadians would be diminished. This is an important part of the Bill to remember because it is a major improvement over what had originally been recommended.

It is important to recognize as well that the generic drug firms, in their discussions with the Minister, actually said that they felt that six years was a time period with which they could quite happily live. The protection is to be only seven years, which is not much longer than they had originally suggested was possible to live with.
The changes the Government has proposed in Bill C-22 provide incentives to generic firms to set up fine chemical manufacturing facilities in Canada to provide earlier access to the market. These provisions will increase employment for Canadians and will increase the availability of Canadian-made drugs to Canadian hospitals and pharmacies and to individual citizens.
The Government is also providing an incentive for Canadian drug research and development in Bill C-22. When a drug has been invented and developed in Canada, that is, when the drug is the product of Canadian research performed in Canada, it will be given protection from imported generic competitors for the full time of the patent. In that way we will again be encouraging the Canadian industry and the development and manufacture of Canadian drugs. To take full advantage of this protection the patentee must manufacture the drug in Canada. If that is not done, after the same seven-year period as for nonCanadian drugs, the generic firms will be able to activate their licences to manufacture the drugs themselves. The difference between the length of the periods of exclusivity for manufacturing and importing licences provides a much greater incentive for manufacturing in Canada and will maximize the employment benefits of Canada.
As I noted earlier, the Drug Prices Review Board will be headed by Dr. Harry Eastman who is, as we all know, one of the foremost outstanding authorities on this industry. This Board will provide a level of protection from excessive drug prices which is far greater than has until now been available to Canadians. The Board, which will have strong powers to call evidence and to pass judgment on the appropriateness of drug prices, will be independent. Its responsibility will be to ensure that Canadians continue to enjoy moderate and reasonable prices for patented drug products.
The provincial Governments, through their constitutional responsibility for the delivery of health care to Canadians and their involvement in drug cost reimbursement plans for their citizens, are the largest purchasers of prescription drugs. The importance of the provincial role in health care and the provision of drugs at reasonable prices is recognized in this Bill. The Drug Prices Review Board will be required to notify the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) and the Ministers responsible for health in the provinces of any hearing which the Board is going to hold. The provinces are in fact being given a statutory right to present evidence to the Board in order to guarantee that they are heard. The Board will have the powers to compel companies to provide evidence on the prices for which they have sold the medicine in Canada and in other countries. When necessary, the Board will take into account the cost of making the medicines and determining
Patent Act
whether the price is appropriate. If the Board, after hearing and reviewing the evidence, decides that the price of a medicine is excessive, it will have the authority to compel the company to reduce the price to whatever level the Board feels is appropriate. As further punitive measures, when the Board deems it appropriate, it will also be able to revoke the exclusivity for a second patented product sold by that company.
It is intended that the Board be able to act quickly in any cases of suspected excessive prices. That is why the Board will be small, consisting of not more than five persons, and will be supported by a secretariat.
The Board will review the prices at which new drugs are introduced, the prices at which they continue to be sold, and will deal with all patent medicines. By giving the Board wide scope in terms of the drugs it can deal with, and stronger powers to call for evidence and enforce its decision, Bill C-22 both extends and solidifies the price protection available to Canadian consumers of patented products.
I am confident that these amendments to the compulsory licensing provisions of the Patent Act will strengthen Canada's position as a participant in pharmaceutical research and development, and I am confident that it will strengthen Canada's pharmaceutical manufacturing centre and continue to provide Canadians with moderate and reasonable drug prices.
My hon. friends opposite should take note of the editorial in The Globe and Mail to which I referred earlier. It states that moving toward normal patent protection for pharmaceuticals is like getting out of rent controls. Opposition Parties fulminate, consumer groups agitate and, in this case, others will add the anti-American view. Fortunately, the Government has both the cause and the powers to do the right thing.

SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY-NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL-ABOLITION OF 200 POSITIONS IN APRIL-GOVERNMENT POSITION. (B) GOVERNMENT FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 15, I raised the now infamous cuts at the National Research Council in a question in the House. On that day officials of the NRC announced at a press conference that they would be cutting $20 million from their budget and provided Canadians with a detailed list of the cuts. That $20 million cut was being made to a budget of some $400 million. The Government had previously cut the budget of the NRC by some $120 million in the two years since it took office. The cuts now total almost 30 per cent of the previous NRC budget of $520 million in November of 1984.
Also on October 15, John Polanyi, Professor of Chemistry at the University of Toronto, won the Nobel Prize. The coincidence of Dr. Polanyi winning the Nobel Prize and the Government cutting further in the area of research and development
Adjournment Debate
caused these issues to appear on the front pages of our newspapers and in the evening telecasts.
As an aside, some Tory Members several weeks later had the audacity to suggest in committee that the NRC had somehow planned to make these cuts on the very day that John Polanyi won the Nobel Prize. They indicated that there was some sort of conspiracy which the NRC had conjured up to try to make the Government look bad. How ludicrous.
I attended the press conference given by the NRC officials. They announced the $20 million in cuts at the direction and under the orders of the Government. The press conference coincided with a meeting of the executive committee of the NRC, following a meeting of the full membership of the council in September. At the end of that rather dreary press conference, I remember a member of the media saying to Larkin Kerwin, the President of the NRC: "Did you know that John Polanyi just won the Nobel Prize?" Dr. Kerwin was pleasantly surprised and somewhat taken aback. How ludicrous it is for members of the Conservative Party to suggest that there was some sort of conspiracy on the part of the NRC to announce the cuts on the same day as Dr. Polanyi won the Nobel Prize.
We know what happened thereafter. There was an outcry from all parts of the country when it was learned that the public safety office at the NRC was being sacrificed. That office had done some work in the area of detection of drugs and bombs at airports. It had done considerable work with police forces across the country. There was a protest from the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police. We also learned that cold weather research would be affected. Work in the area of icing of structures in the North, such as transmission lines and helicopter blades, is going down the drain. We learned that the work of the scientists who had developed the mechanism which controls the Canadarm was being cut out.
We were told by the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) that there would be no lay-offs at the NRC. Several days later he told us that there would be no lay-offs this year. After that he said he personally would try to place scientists in universities and in the private sector to prove that there would be no lay-offs. The truth is somewhat different than what we were told by the Minister. We were told by officials at NRC that all the fat had been cut out in the past several years and that it would be difficult to avoid layoffs this time around.
I could talk about the effect on morale of people at the NRC which is at all-time low, however, I would like to conclude by saying that the Minister's tactical retreat is unsatisfactory. The Minister has named a task force to review the cuts, but he has not said that it has the authority to reverse the cuts. He has not said that the Government will restore the funding of $20 million to the National Research Council. That is what I ask the Minister to do today, and I hope all Canadians will send him a message to that effect.

November 24, 1986

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the chance to reply to the Member's question because it gives me an opportunity to set the record straight and lay to rest many of the exaggerated and unfair statements raised recently.
First, the extent of the reductions has been exaggerated. The Hon. Member said that the cut was 30 per cent when in actual fact it is only 9 per cent.

subtopic: SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY-NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL-ABOLITION OF 200 POSITIONS IN APRIL-GOVERNMENT POSITION. (B) GOVERNMENT FUNDING
speechtext: Take a look at your estimates.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY-NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL-ABOLITION OF 200 POSITIONS IN APRIL-GOVERNMENT POSITION. (B) GOVERNMENT FUNDING
speechtext:
An area of gross exaggeration has been the impact on people. It has been claimed that the reductions affect some 200 positions. In actual fact, as the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger) found out in the Standing Committee, only 184 people are directly affected, something like half of them will be reassigned before the end of the year and the remainder will have a minimum of 13 months more in which to find satisfactory work. NRC expects to use many innovative ways to help these people. For example, the NRC wind tunnel will be commercialized and actively marketed. This could actually result in an expansion of employment at the facility if it goes to two shifts per day.
NRC is also discussing the possibility of transferring various research teams to Canadian universities or other departments so that they can maintain their R and D activities with limited disruptions. NSERC funding may be provided to help ease the transition.
NRC has also imposed a freeze on outside hiring, and an early retirement program will be introduced. All together these actions will ensure that valuable research and technical resources remain effectively utilized, even if they are not employed by the NRC. Finally, NRC will be getting additional person-years for some programs so that by next year their person-year authorities will be expanding.
Another issue that has often been raised is the question of IRAP. In spite of everything the Opposition has said, it can now be confirmed that IRAP contributions will not be reduced. We have always recognized how important that program is and have never wanted to cut it.
Lastly, many people have raised concerns over certain specific reductions. Many problems have been raised and a variety of dangers alluded to. We have now appointed a task force with three eminent persons to review the reductions to ensure that no such problems arise. In sum, the reductions and reallocations at NRC are only part of the Government's program in science and technology. They can be seen as necessary and important redress from the situation we inherited. The NRC situation has been exaggerated out of proportion. In actual fact, the extent of the cuts is not very great, the impact on people has been contained and the NRC remains a strong and viable research facility with new resources in important areas like biotechnology and space.
I recognize that the Hon. Member did not have the courtesy to remain for the answer.

BANKS AND BANKING-ESTEY COMMISSION REPORT-NONPUBLICATION OF UNINSURED DEPOSITORS' NAMES. (B) INQUIRY CONCERNING POSSIBLE INTERIM REPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the report of the Estey commission was released last month, I have asked a number of questions concerning the uninsured and as yet unnamed Canadian Commercial Bank and Northland Bank depositors who were fully reimbursed by the Government out of public funds. For over a year now my colleagues and I have been asking the Government to justify its refusal to release the names of those uninsured depositors who received nearly $1 billion in ex gratia payments out of the public purse. I would remind the House that these are the so-called sophisticated investors since we are talking about a wholesale bank. In fact, at least one investor on the secret list received $1 million of taxpayers' money to compensate for a lost deposit.
First the Government said that the provisions of the Bank Act precluded it from releasing the names. However, when my colleagues and I asked exactly what portion of the Bank Act and asked to see the legal opinions on which the Government was basing its interpretation of the Bank Act, we received no answers. I also asked why the Government was citing the Bank Act in the first place since the situation involved former banks then in liquidation whose affairs might reasonably be considered to be subject to the provisions of the Winding-Up Act rather than the Bank Act. Again I received no answer.
Finally, on October 1, 1985, I was told by the former Minister of State (Finance), as reported at page 7206 of Hansard:
-I am quite prepared to release the lists to the commission and have Mr. Justice Estey decide-
We now have the report of the Estey commission and, as illuminating and thorough as it is, it is completely silent on the matter of the uninsured depositors. On October 31, 1986, when I pursued this with the current Minister of State (Finance) (Mr. Hockin) he said, as reported at page 950 of Hansard:
-when the commission was established the question of the names of depositors was something on which Mr. Justice Estey was to decide .... It is not now our position to challenge Justice Estey's decision since it was his decision. He received the names and he has decided not to publish them.
When I pursued this further on November 3, 1986, I received a different response from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) who said, as reported at page 1007 of Hansard:
We decided it was inappropriate for us to release those names ... We know that the matter could have been considered by Mr. Justice Estey. He chose not to do so.
In fact, we now know that the matter was never referred to Mr. Justice Estey. It was never a part of his terms of reference. Finally, after 18 months, the Minster of Finance admitted that it was his decision and that of his Cabinet colleagues and was
November 24, 1986

not particularly based on a legal opinion or on Mr. Justice Estey or anyone else behind whom they had tried to hide.
I do not think that Canadian taxpayers, who surely have the right to know where their tax dollars are going, will accept that the matter rests there. We in the Official Opposition have always taken the position that taxpayers have the right to know and we agree with the former Deputy Prime Minister who said in this House on October 4, 1985, as reported at page 7332 of Hansard-.
-public funds are at all times subject to the scrutiny of Parliament. That is what this place is all about.
However, the Government has been less than forthcoming and has contradicted itself in the little that has been said. First we were told that there was a decision on the part of the Estey Commission not to release the names of the uninsured depositors. Then we were told that in fact it was the Government's decision and that the matter was not considered by the commission and was never part of its terms of reference.
It is not acceptable for the Minister of Finance to say, as he did on November 3, that it was the Government's decision not to release the names and to attempt to close the book on it without any reasonable explanation. A secret list of people who got $875 million from the taxpayers' pockets requires a very full explanation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gordon Towers (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING-ESTEY COMMISSION REPORT-NONPUBLICATION OF UNINSURED DEPOSITORS' NAMES. (B) INQUIRY CONCERNING POSSIBLE INTERIM REPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has raised the question of the publication of the list of uninsured depositors of the CCB and Northland Bank who were compensated under Bill C-79.
As was indicated in the House last fall, and reiterated this month, the Government felt it would be inappropriate to release the names of the uninsured depositors of the two banks because it holds as an important principle respect for the privacy rights of individuals. Protection of this privacy is consistent with the intent of the Bank Act and the Access to Information Act. The private financial information given by a depositor to a bank is given in confidence and treated with confidence from that moment forward under the privacy provisions of the Bank Act. Such protection of the privacy of individuals continues to be the position of the Government.
While the Government protected the names of depositors, it did table in the House a detailed breakdown of the categories of depositors compensated under Bill C-79. These lists were organized into more than 40 categories for each institution, representing a very clear and concise picture of the individuals and types of organizations who received compensation under the Bill. The breakdown clearly demonstrated therefore where and to what major groups in society the funds were to be paid. By doing so, the Government acted responsibly in providing as much information as possible, and at the same time did not violate the right to privacy of uninsured depositors.
Adjournment Debate
The Government, while it did not feel entitled to release the names of uninsured depositors, did send the list of these individuals to Mr. Justice Estey. I want to clarify to the House, however, that the list was provided to the commission as part of a package of background information regarding events related to the Canadian Commercial Bank and Northland Bank failures. Mr. Estey was not asked to decide whether or not the list of uninsured depositors should be made public.

PHARMACEUTICAL INDUSTRY-STATEMENT ATTRIBUTED TO UNITED STATES TRADE NEGOTIATOR. (B) CONSUMER ASSOCIATION'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 19 I put a question to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) with regard to a statement by the U.S. special trade representative on whether drug prices will rise as the result of the Government's legislation. Of course, the answer is that Mr. Yeutter said drug prices will rise. According to the transcript of the program, he said:
Any improvements in this area are clearly in the best interest of Canada as a nation. Now in some cases maybe this will raise the price at the retail level of some of these products, but if we're going to have low retail prices based upon piracy it seems to me that's not a sound way to run a country.
My point was simply that if Clayton Yeutter said drug prices will rise and if Professor Eastman and the Canadian Drug Manufacturers Association said drug prices will rise, then there is not much doubt.
I realize that the Minister valiantly held out by insisting that the savings Canadians would make would come in the form of lower prices rather than higher prices, but he too finally conceded the point on Friday when he said his "worst case scenario" meant that drug prices could rise. I wonder if this could be confirmed tonight? I asked again in Question Period this afternoon, and I did not get any real answer, as to how much prices will rise as a result of this Bill.
The second part of Mr. Yeutter's comments was the reference to Canadian policy being based on piracy. Canadian patent rules are based on our national needs within recognized international conventions. They have withstood the many challenges which the multinational companies have made, the most recent being the Federal Court decision of 1985 which found that Canada's drug patent law was not an abridgement of the freedoms granted under the Canadian Charter of Rights, and further had not stopped the companies from earning substantial profits.
Compulsory licences, which authorized generics in this country, are a well-known patent device. They are recognized as such and the only reason they are being restricted, as proposed in this Bill, is not because they are theft, piracy, or that the people who apply for them are scavengers, but that the United States does not like them.
To change the present policy is to say that we must act like the big boys who are our trading partners. It ignores the fact that Canada is a very small minnow in the world drug market.

November 24, 1986
Adjournment Debate
We are 2 per cent of that market. There are no multinationals with headquarters in Canada. All the indigenous Canadian drug companies have largely been bought up by multinationals and often had their research transferred to the United States.
Faced with this situation, the Government made the right choice in 1969. It said that we will not get much in the way of research and employment in an industry that is not employment intensive, so we have opted for lower prices and a smaller indigenous generic industry.
It is another form of the Auto Pact where we have recognized international reality and made the best deal for ourselves. The Government's legislation will now sacrifice both these aspects of a successful drug policy. I invite the Member who replies on behalf of the Government to confirm that we will no longer have low prices as our policy goal in prescription drugs, that we will have a generic drug industry which will be stalled for at least seven years before it has new drugs to produce and we will have a system which is essentially like that of the United States. Certainly Clayton Yeutter will be happy, but most Canadians will not be. I invite the Government to recognize why Canadians are not happy and why the majority is so opposed to this Bill.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Gabrielle Bertrand (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: PHARMACEUTICAL INDUSTRY-STATEMENT ATTRIBUTED TO UNITED STATES TRADE NEGOTIATOR. (B) CONSUMER ASSOCIATION'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), who has quoted Mr. Yeutter, I would like to say that perhaps there is some misunderstanding about the contents of this bill and about the role and functions of the Patented Medicine Prices Review Board. As the Minister has said on numerous occasions, this Bill will not affect drugs now sold in Canada and will not cause any increase in their price. The drugs which now have generic equivalents will continue to have them and competition between the manufacturer of innovative products and the generic company will continue to guarantee low prices for these products.
In the case of all existing drugs for which there is no generic equivalent at this time and of new drugs marketed in the future, the Prices Review Board is empowered to guarantee that the prices are reasonable and that any increase corresponds to the Consumer Price Index.
The Patented Medicine Prices Review Board is also empowered to compare the prices asked for a drug in Canada with those asked in other countries and to ensure that prices in Canada are reasonable and fair to Canadians. When the Board identifies an unreasonable price, it will have the power to revoke the exclusivity period for the product involved, and in extreme cases, to remove the exclusivity of another product of the same manufacturer.
Mr. Yeutter used the word piracy. I strongly oppose any allegation that our compulsory licensing system is an illegal counterfeiting scheme. The changes which will be made under Bill C-22 had long been suggested by other OECD countries. The previous Government had started a review process and corrections are now being made to our compulsory licensing policy, not as a response to these accusations, but because the Government wants to encourage investment in pharmaceutical research and development in this country. The Government wants also to stimulate the growth of a high quality chemical product branch in the pharmaceutical industry. The current policy has made very little progress on either of these fronts and the changes Bill C-22 will bring about will help remedy the situation. This initiative will create at least 3,000 new jobs for Canadians and will attract huge investments in research, development and manufacturing in the pharmaceutical industry in Canada.
